clue.text: Weapons, used in the Amazon wars?

definitions.text: Weapons, used in the Amazon wars?

parts.words: Weapons, used in the Amazon wars?
parts.note: the Amazons were a nation of warrior women, so in their wars the blades would be busy slicing at girls: the swords split as a phrase into 'cut' and 'lasses'

explanation.surface: A question about which blades were wielded in battles along the South American river.
explanation.walkthrough: The Amazon here is not the river but the legendary race of female warriors; their wars are fought among women, so the weapons are what 'cut lasses'.
explanation.definitionFit: These are short curved swords once carried by sailors and pirates, so they are weapons.

clue.text: Successful competitor at teatime

parts.note: a champion holds a trophy cup, and anyone drinking tea holds a teacup

explanation.surface: A winner at the tea table.
explanation.walkthrough: A cup-holder is a champion who holds the trophy; at teatime, anyone holding a teacup fits the description too.
explanation.definitionFit: The holder of a trophy is the winner of a competition.

clue.text: Graceful form of comedy

parts.note: Thalia was both the Muse of comedy and one of the three Graces, so an adjective from her name is both comic and 'Graceful'

explanation.surface: An elegant style of comic writing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Graceful' means belonging to the Graces: Thalia was one of them and also the Muse of comedy.
explanation.definitionFit: Relating to Thalia, the Muse of comedy, the adjective means comic.

clue.text: They don't speak for themselves

parts.note: lawyers argue on behalf of clients, never for themselves

explanation.surface: A remark about shy people who let others talk.
explanation.walkthrough: It seems to describe shy people; it means lawyers, who speak for their clients.
explanation.definitionFit: Lawyers act and speak on behalf of others.

clue.text: A boom in coins, perhaps

definitions.note: a boom is a loud sound, which this adjective describes, as in a sonic boom

indicators.note: perhaps shows the letters of the coins could be arranged another way

explanation.surface: A rise in the value of money.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Boom' suggests a surge in coin prices; it is the noise of a sonic boom. 'perhaps' rearranges COINS.
explanation.definitionFit: A sonic boom is the noise of a supersonic aircraft, so the adjective relates to sound waves.

clue.text: Support for us in prodigal surroundings

indicators.note: in means placed within, so the word for us goes into the other word
surroundings means the word for the prodigal is wrapped around the other

parts.note: a prodigal is a spendthrift, a spender
taken as written

explanation.surface: Help for us amid an extravagant background.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Support' sounds structural; it is the strap holding up a stocking. 'prodigal' is a noun here, the spendthrift, not an adjective on 'surroundings'.
explanation.definitionFit: A suspender is a strap that holds up stockings or socks, so it is a support.

clue.text: Present for Christmas or Boxing Day ?

definitions.meaning: a pair of woollen foot coverings is a classic festive gift
on a day of boxing the fighters land punches, which are informally called by this word

explanation.surface: Wondering whether a gift belongs to the 25th or the day after.
explanation.walkthrough: Boxing Day, 26 December, is a British public holiday; read literally as a day of boxing, it is full of punches.
explanation.definitionFit: Hosiery is a stock stocking-filler gift, and as a verb or plural noun the word also means blows from a fist.

clue.text: A little girl gets little work in this county

parts.note: Sal is a short name for a girl (Sally, Sarah)
op is short for opus, a work

explanation.surface: A child earning a small wage in a rural shire.
explanation.walkthrough: Salop is the old name for Shropshire, an English county.
explanation.definitionFit: Salop is the former official name of Shropshire, an English county.

clue.text: Farewell to a vessel in song

indicators.note: to means attached onto, so the goodbye is put after the vessel

parts.note: a can is a container or vessel
ta-ta is an informal goodbye

explanation.surface: Bidding goodbye to a ship by singing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'vessel' suggests a ship being waved off, but it is a mere tin; ta-ta is a British colloquial goodbye. 'in' is a link word.
explanation.definitionFit: A cantata is a sung choral work, so a song.

clue.text: Something to do with utter confidence

definitions.text: Something to do with utter confidence

parts.words: Something to do with utter confidence
parts.note: utter means to say, and confidence is a secret: to say something in confidence; utter is the verb, not 'total'

explanation.surface: An act carried out with complete self-assurance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'utter' looks like an adjective meaning total; it is the verb meaning to say.
explanation.definitionFit: To utter something is to voice it aloud, the same as talking.

clue.text: God-like carriage

definitions.meaning: Phaethon (also spelt this way) was the son of the sun god Helios who drove his father's chariot
a light open four-wheeled horse-drawn carriage bears this name

explanation.surface: A description of a vehicle worthy of a deity.
explanation.definitionFit: The mythical son of the sun god shares his name with an open horse-drawn coach, named after his chariot ride.

clue.text: Great Dane's inaudible last word

parts.note: the great Dane is Hamlet, Prince of Denmark, whose dying words are 'The rest is ...', ending on a word for the absence of sound

explanation.surface: A dog breed's final, unheard utterance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Great Dane' suggests the dog; it is Hamlet, whose last line in Shakespeare is 'The rest is silence', a word that is itself soundless.
explanation.definitionFit: Hamlet's final word names quiet, the complete absence of any audible noise.

clue.text: " O, willow, willow " as a Cockney tradesman might say ?

indicators.note: Cockney speech famously drops the opening aitch of a word, so the H at the start is lost
the tradesman's title is given as a Londoner would pronounce it, without its first letter

parts.note: a hosier is a tradesman who sells stockings and socks

explanation.surface: Desdemona's willow song quoted in the accent of an East End shopkeeper.
explanation.walkthrough: 'O, willow, willow' echoes Desdemona's willow song in Othello. A Cockney (East Londoner) drops the H of HOSIER, leaving OSIER.
explanation.definitionFit: An osier is a kind of willow whose pliant shoots are used in basket-making.

clue.text: He's not necessarily a worthless knave

definitions.text: He's not necessarily a worthless knave

parts.words: He's not necessarily a worthless knave
parts.note: split the term into 'cheap' (worthless) and 'jack' (the knave in cards); yet the man so called is only a pedlar of low-priced goods, not a scoundrel

explanation.surface: A defence of someone's character against a charge of villainy.
explanation.walkthrough: The jack in a pack of cards is also called the knave, so 'cheap jack' looks like 'worthless knave'; the real meaning is merely a hawker of cheap wares.
explanation.definitionFit: A cheapjack is a travelling seller of inexpensive goods, a trader rather than a rogue.

clue.text: Heard in a hop-garden ?

parts.note: a hop is an informal dance, so a hop-garden is read as an outdoor dance venue where a group of musicians would be playing

explanation.surface: Wondering what sounds carry across a field where hops are grown for beer.
explanation.walkthrough: A hop-garden is a field growing hops for brewing; here 'hop' is a dance, so what is heard is the music group.
explanation.definitionFit: A band playing music for dancing is what one hears at a dance, or hop.

clue.text: Port or spirit ? Take your choice

definitions.meaning: Arkhangelsk, a northern Russian seaport, is known in English by this name
a chief angel is a spiritual being

explanation.surface: Offering a choice of drinks, a fortified wine or a strong liquor.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Port' and 'spirit' look like drinks; one is a Russian seaport, the other a heavenly being.
explanation.definitionFit: A Russian White Sea harbour bears the name of a chief angel, a heavenly being.

clue.text: Song for David's day ?

parts.note: King David is traditionally credited with the sacred songs of the Old Testament, so a song in his day was a hymn of that kind

explanation.surface: A tune to celebrate St David's Day, Wales's national day.
explanation.walkthrough: St David's Day (1 March) is the Welsh national day, but the David meant is the biblical king, author of the Psalms.
explanation.definitionFit: The Book of Psalms holds sacred songs traditionally attributed to King David.

clue.text: Pictorial dispatches perhaps

parts.note: cards with a picture on one side sent through the mail

explanation.surface: Illustrated war reports.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dispatches' suggests military reports; it means items sent by post.
explanation.definitionFit: Picture cards sent through the mail are messages with an image.

clue.text: Parasite much in evidence at 19

parts.note: a parasitic plant growing on trees, hung as a decoration in the festive season of the 19-across answer

explanation.surface: A pest that shows up a great deal at a certain time of year.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue refers to 19-across: the parasitic plant is hung up at that festive season, for kissing under.
explanation.definitionFit: This white-berried plant grows as a parasite on trees and is a traditional festive decoration.

clue.text: Puzzle concerning public transport

parts.note: re is a short word meaning about or concerning
a bus is a vehicle of public transport

explanation.surface: A brain-teaser about buses and trains.
explanation.definitionFit: A rebus is a picture puzzle where images or letters stand for words.

clue.text: A bitter could go to one's head

definitions.text: A bitter could go to one's head

indicators.note: could go suggests the letters of the beer may travel into a different order

explanation.surface: A pint of beer might make you tipsy.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is about beer going to the head; 'could go' rearranges A BITTER into a square clerical cap, which goes on one's head.
explanation.definitionFit: A biretta is a square cap worn by Catholic clergy, so it is worn on the head.

clue.text: One season, anyhow, has its charms

indicators.note: anyhow means in any haphazard way, so the letters of the words that follow are thrown into a new order

explanation.surface: Every time of year, in its own way, has something appealing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'anyhow' signals rearranging ITS CHARMS; 'has' links the definition to the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: The festive period at the end of December is a season of the year.

clue.text: State of a man not upset

indicators.note: upset means knocked over, so the letters of the words are tipped into a new order

explanation.surface: The condition of a man who stays calm.
explanation.walkthrough: 'State' looks like condition; it is a US state. 'upset' rearranges A MAN NOT; 'of' links.
explanation.definitionFit: Montana is a state in the north-western United States.

clue.text: The earliest known means of identification

definitions.text: The earliest known means of identification

parts.words: The earliest known means of identification
parts.note: a mark present on the skin from the moment one is born, so it identifies a person from their very first day

explanation.surface: A historian's note on the oldest system for telling people apart.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Earliest known' sounds like ancient history; it means present since birth.
explanation.definitionFit: A blemish on the skin carried since birth can be used to identify a person.

clue.text: Judicial form

parts.note: a form is a long seat, and the seat of judges is called by this word

explanation.surface: A legal document.
explanation.walkthrough: 'form' suggests paperwork; a form is also a backless bench seat, and judges collectively are the bench.
explanation.definitionFit: Judges sit on a long seat, and the term stands for the judiciary.

clue.text: They get what's left

parts.note: those who inherit receive what someone has left in a will

explanation.surface: People who must take the leftovers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'what's left' seems to mean leftovers; it is what is bequeathed.
explanation.definitionFit: Inheritors receive what a dead person bequeaths.

clue.text: Just the lad to know about six

indicators.note: about means around, so the word for knowing goes round the numeral

parts.note: ken means to know, as in Scottish and northern dialect
VI is six in Roman numerals

explanation.surface: A boy who knows about the number six.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Just the lad' means simply a boy's name; ken (to know) is Scottish dialect, as in 'beyond my ken'.
explanation.definitionFit: Kevin is a boy's given name, a lad.

clue.text: One way to question the ability of nearly everyone

parts.note: asking 'can ...?' questions whether someone is able

indicators.note: nearly means not quite complete, so the last letter of the word for everyone is lost

parts.note: everyone is all

explanation.surface: A method of doubting whether the whole population is capable.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Can all?' asks whether everyone is able; 'nearly' cuts the last letter of ALL.
explanation.definitionFit: A canal is an artificial waterway, a route for boats.

clue.text: Love of games

parts.note: in tennis and similar games 'love' is a score of zero

explanation.surface: Fondness for sport.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Love' looks like affection; in game scoring it means a score of nil.
explanation.definitionFit: A love score in tennis means zero, the same as no points at all.

clue.text: Sport that includes a song ?

parts.note: a sport in biology is an organism that differs from its parent type, and the word for that holds the operatic solo ARIA within it

explanation.surface: Asking which game has singing as part of it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sport' is not a game: in biology a sport is a mutation or odd form, and the word meaning that contains ARIA, a song.
explanation.definitionFit: A sport in biology is an offshoot differing from its type, also called a deviant form.

clue.text: They should be warmly contested

parts.note: preliminary rounds of a race are fought keenly, and their name also means bouts of warmth

explanation.surface: A remark on matters that ought to provoke heated debate.
explanation.walkthrough: Heats are qualifying races; the word also means warmth, hence 'warmly'.
explanation.definitionFit: Qualifying races in a competition are called by the same word as spells of warmth.

clue.text: Not the view of the lonely ancient mariner

definitions.text: Not the view of the lonely ancient mariner

parts.words: Not the view of the lonely ancient mariner
parts.note: Coleridge's Ancient Mariner was 'alone on a wide wide sea', so all he saw was water, never a scene of countryside

explanation.surface: A remark about what Coleridge's sailor did not see.
explanation.walkthrough: Coleridge's Ancient Mariner saw only the sea (a seascape), never the countryside on land.
explanation.definitionFit: A view of countryside on land is the opposite of a seascape that a sailor would see.
